COVID-19 will weigh on activity and elevate downside risks, but the FOMC’s immediate cut to the 0–1/4% range and “at least” $700B in Treasury and MBS purchases—along with expanded repos, discount window easing, reserve requirement changes, and global dollar swap lines—is a textbook countercyclical response aimed at stabilizing credit and expectations. This toolkit targets the credit channel by lowering external finance premia and easing balance-sheet constraints, consistent with evidence from Oliner and Rudebusch (1996a), Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein (1994), and Gertler and Gilchrist (1994), and supports bank lending when market-based funding strains intensify. With market-based inflation compensation falling but surveys little changed, anchoring expectations via forceful easing and guidance aligns with Svensson’s inflation-forecast targeting framework and helps avoid liquidity-trap/deflation dynamics flagged in the literature. VAR evidence (Sims, 1992) and broader macro studies show such interventions can cushion output even near the effective lower bound. Netting these insights, the near-term outlook remains negative due to the pandemic shock, but the policy stance materially mitigates its depth and persistence.
